text: Nonconvergence in Bayesian estimation of migration rates. The estimation of migration rates using molecular markers is an important aspect of many population genetic studies. Several different methods are available for estimating migration, but most of these make multiple limiting assumptions. One method that is relatively free from assumptions is BAYESASS, which uses assignment methods in a Bayesian framework. However, when tested using simulated data, this method was found to have problems with the convergence of the Markov chain Monte Carlo. Here, I perform a literature study to test whether these convergence problems are also present when BAYESASS is used to estimate migration rates from empirical data. A review of 100 studies that have used BAYESASS shows that this is indeed the case. The estimated proportions of nonmigrants were mostly either close to 2/3 or 1, indicating that the MCMC tends to get trapped near the bounds of the prior distribution. In addition, I found that the quality of the inference was negatively affected by the number of sampled populations, but increased with increasing numbers of sampled individuals and with the strength of the population structure as measured by FST. Based on these results, I give several recommendations that should help to reduce problems when using BAYESASS with empirical data. Most importantly, I argue that researchers should be more realistic about inferences of migration rates and that BAYESASS will give optimal results only when the experiment has been especially designed around its use.

Migration among populations is a major driving force in evolution and one of the main concepts in population genetics (Abdo et al. 2004). High migration rates may prevent or erode local adaptation and even blur species borders. Low migration rates can cause strong differentiation between populations, create clines in allele frequencies, provide a starting point for speciation and also hamper the spread of beneficial new mutations. Therefore, measuring rates of gene flow is an important aspect of studies on adaptation, speciation, molecular evolution and conservation biology. The burgeoning field of landscape genetics (Manel et al. 2010) essentially entails studying how landscape features (often man-made ones) influence patterns of gene flow across populations.

Indirect methods that use molecular genetic markers are nowadays the preferred way of estimating migration rates. This is because direct measurement of migration using mark–release–recapture is time-consuming, difficult and in fact only possible for a relatively small number of larger animal species. Indirect methods are less labour-intensive, applicable to all kinds of organisms and may pick up the effects of rare long-distance dispersal events that are very difficult to measure using direct methods. Together with the increasing efficiency and power of molecular tools, statistical tools for estimating migration have become increasingly sophisticated. However, these tools depend on a large number of – often unrealistic– assumptions, such as equilibrium between migration, mutation and drift (Beerli & Felsenstein 1999; Whitlock & McCauley 1999).

The program BAYESASS (Wilson & Rannala 2003) presents an elegant method for the estimation of migration rates. Its unique selling point is that it is not dependent on the assumption of equilibrium and makes few other assumptions about the underlying population or mutation model. The estimated migration rates can be asymmetric, which is, for example, useful for detecting source-sink dynamics in natural populations. Though the markers are assumed to be in linkage equilibrium, BAYESASS can also be used on populations that are not in Correspondence: Patrick G. Because of these qualities, BAYESASS has become widely used and is now a part of the standard statistical toolbox of molecular ecologists.

BAYESASS works by looking for individuals with migrant ancestry in the population samples. When the migration rate is low, the frequency of individuals with a single migrant ancestor is a linear function of the migration rate m: direct migrants have frequency m, individuals with one migrant parent have frequency 2 m, etc. The frequencies of other combinations, such as individuals with two migrant parents, are of order m2 and higher. However, when m is low, these higher-order terms can be neglected. Manel et al. 2005) to find individuals with migrant ancestry, restricting itself to individuals with a single migrant ancestor from the last two generations of migration. It then uses the frequency of such individuals to estimate m in a Bayesian framework with a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), concurrently estimating the allele frequencies and the inbreeding coefficient F. However, this requires that the allele frequencies are stable over the last few generations and not altered by genetic drift or migration. Despite being applicable to nonequilibrium situations, BAYESASS obviously does make several assumptions. Most importantly, it assumes that migration rates are low, for two different reasons: first, the migration rate has to be low enough so that mating between individuals with migrant ancestry does not take place; second, too high migration rates will change the allele frequencies over short time periods. The method therefore has a hard limit where the proportion of nonmigrants in a population cannot be lower than 2/3, which means that the maximum pairwise migration rate is 1/3. However, also at this maximum migration rate, the assumption of low migration rates is violated for both reasons. When m = 1/3, only 30% of the individuals in the population have no migrant ancestry, which means that mating between individuals with migrant ancestry will be common. Furthermore, such a level of migration will have a drastic short-term effect on the allele frequencies. When discussing this assumption, Wilson & Rannala (2003) state that at FST = 0.05, a migration rate of m < 0.05 will make sure that changes in allele frequencies are negligibly small. (2007) suggest that m < 0.1 is needed to ensure demographic independence of populations (based on Hastings 1993). Two studies have assessed the performance of BAYESASS for the estimation of migration rates. Mardulyn et al. (2008) used an experimental set-up with controlled migration among laboratory cultures of Caenorhabditis elegans. They found that the estimates provided by BAYESASS were generally overestimates, even though the real values were within the reported confidence interval.

(2007) used computer simulations and found that in general, the residual mean square error (RMSE) of the estimates was lowest with higher values of FST, higher numbers of loci and larger sample sizes. However, the RMSE increased with an increase in the number of sampled populations. When the simulations matched the inference model, they found that BAYESASS gave “fairly accurate” estimates of migration rates up to 0.1 when the population differentiation is moderately low (FST ≥0.05). However, when the simulation model did not exactly match the inference model, but were performed using the program EasyPop (Balloux 2001), the migration estimates were much less accurate. In that case, accurate estimates of the migration rate were only obtained when the migration rates were low (m = 0.01) and differentiation was strong (FST ≥0.1). Importantly, Faubet et al. (2007) noticed convergence problems of the MCMC for the simulations that did not match the inference model. They observed that the MCMC often got trapped around values close to the fixed minimum and maximum values of 2/3 and 1. They concluded that when the demographic history of the populations does not match the inference model of the method, extreme caution should be taken in the interpretation of the results from BAYESASS. They advised that in order to minimize such convergence problems, all analyses using BAYESASS should perform multiple repeat runs of the MCMC and use the Bayesian deviance (see Spiegelhalter et al. 2002) to select the run to use for parameter estimation. However, it is important to verify whether such convergence problems are also present when BAYESASS is used to estimate migration rates from empirical data. Here, I perform a literature study to analyse the quality of BAYESASS inferences performed using empirical data. I look for signs of nonconvergence by looking at the distribution of migration estimates to see whether the MCMC gets trapped near the bounds of the prior distribution. I also test whether the incidence of such problems is related to parameters of the study design (numbers of populations, loci, and individuals) and the analysis (FST, length of the MCMC, and the number of repeat runs). I finish by giving some recommendations for the use of BAYESASS that will help to minimize such problems.

Out of the more than 550 studies that have cited the original work by Wilson & Rannala (2003), I selected 100 studies that have used BAYESASS to estimate migration rates (see Table S1, Supporting information for a full list of references). I selected only studies with a clear, tabular presentation of the migration estimates. Furthermore, NONCONVERGENCE IN MIGRATION ESTIMATION 727 only studies published in 2008 or later were selected: at least one year after publication of the study by Faubet et al. In total, there were several hundreds of studies that conformed to these criteria, but I restricted myself to the first 100 suitable studies returned by Google Scholar. Some of the selected studies analysed multiple species or separate data sets for a single species, others analysed a single data set in different ways; those were all included as separate entries in the database (when excluding the 7 reanalyses of the same data, the conclusions are the same). In addition, some species were analysed in more than one study. In total, the 100 selected studies presented 122 different analyses on 100 species, resulting in 769 estimates of nonmigrant proportions (see Table S1, Supporting information). From the reported estimates of the migration rates, I focused per population on the nonmigrant proportion: the fraction of the individuals in a population that are not migrants from another population. This gives a single estimate per population and is more convenient for further analyses than the pairwise among-population migration rates. Together with the migration estimates, I collected several characteristics of the studies including the number of populations sampled, the number of individuals for every population, the number of loci, the length of the MCMC chain used, the burn-in of the MCMC chain, the number of repeated runs of BAYESASS and whether the authors made any adjustment of BAYESASS’ Delta parameters. I also gathered any reported overall FST-values; when instead of an overall FST estimate, a table of pairwise FST -values was presented, I took the average of these. The significance of the relationship between the quality of the BAYESASS analysis (see below) and the study parameters was tested by permutation using the function “lmp” from the R-package “lmPerm”.

The literature study shows that there are indeed signs of convergence problems when BAYESASS is used with empirical data. The distribution of the estimates of the nonmigrant proportion shows a clear bimodal distribution with one peak close to the maximum value of 1.0 and one peak close to the fixed minimum value of 2/3 (Fig. 1). In fact, 34% of the estimates were within 10% of the fixed minimum (so <0.73, dotted line in Fig. 1), and 48% of the estimates were within 10% of the fixed maximum (>0.9). The bimodality in Fig. 1 suggests that that the MCMC got trapped near the bounds of the prior distribution as a result of nonconvergence. Less than half (49%) of the selected studies ran multiple runs of BAYESASS with different random number seeds to check for consistency. Of these, only a few studies gave a detailed overview of the consistency between runs. When the results were consistent, this usually was reported, but inconsistency of the results was mostly not discussed at length. Authors used different strategies to handle inconsistent output: some authors only reported the results of the run with the highest log likelihood; more frequently, authors reported the average of the migration estimates from the different repeats. Surprisingly, only three studies used the Bayesian deviance as a measure of model fit. One of those three studies was the one by Rong et al. (2013), who found that among 36 runs, those with higher values of the deviance always had one or multiple nonmigrant rates close to the minimum of 0.67 (J. Rong, personal communication). The run with the lowest deviance, which was selected for interpretation, did not show such signs of nonconvergence.

I found only a single study that clearly showed and discussed the inconsistency of the results from different repeats (Hereward et al. 2013). They presented a graphical overview of the results from ten repeated runs (therefore, their study was not included among the 100 selected studies) and also presented the complete migration tables from all ten repeats in the supplementary material. I retrieved these values and plotted the estimates of the nonmigrant proportions of the ten repeats for every population (Fig. 2). This plot provides a very good illustration of the nonconvergence problems of BAYESASS. For some populations, the estimates are consistently close to the lower bound of 0.67 or the upper bound of 1.0. However, for seven of the thirteen populations studied, the estimates switch between the upper and lower bounds between replicates. No two repeats of the analysis of Hereward et al. (2013) show similar results and, in every repeat, there are at least six populations with estimates that show attraction to the lower bound.

As the nonconvergence of the MCMC chain leads to an attraction to the bounds of the prior distribution, this can be used as a way to assess the quality of BAYESASS results. For each of the 122 datasets, I calculated the fraction of populations that had a nonmigrant proportion within 10% of the lower bound (so below 0.73). This fraction ranged from zero (high quality; none of the population estimates showed attraction to the lower bound) to 0.85 (low quality; almost all population estimates showed such attraction). However, it is important to note that this fraction can only serve as a very rough estimate of the quality of the analysis, as we do not know which of the populations actually have true nonmigrant proportions at this level. The fraction of estimates attracted to the lower bound was negatively correlated with the number of populations sampled (P < 0.001, Fig. 3a). The fraction of estimates attracted to the lower bound was not related to the number of loci (n.s., Fig. The fraction of estimates attracted to the lower bound did decrease slightly with an increasing value of FST (P = 0.012, Fig. 3d). This is expected as a higher value of FST means a stronger differentiation in allele frequencies, which makes it easier to accurately detect migrants. However, the correlation with FST was not as strong as could have been expected. There were several studies with FST > 0.3 where multiple estimates were attracted to the lower bound of the prior distribution. There was no significant effect of the length of the MCMC chain, the length of the burn-in period or the adjustment of the delta values on the fraction of estimates attracted to the lower bound (not shown). In addition, there also was no effect of whether authors used multiple repeats on the fraction of estimates attracted to the lower bound (not shown).

Part of the attraction of BAYESASS (Wilson & Rannala 2003) is that it makes relatively few assumptions and can be used with populations that are not in migration-drift or Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. This stands in contrast to other methods that do make a large number of very stringent assumptions; for example, the once popular method of calculating migration rates directly from FST-values (Wright 1931; Whitlock & McCauley 1999). Nevertheless, the presented literature study makes it clear that also the use of BAYESASS is not without pitfalls: the estimated proportions of nonmigrants show a clear bimodal distribution. It is unlikely that this bimodality is due to the shape of the distribution of the underlying true migration rates; in that case, there would be no effect of the number of population samples on the frequency of estimates that are close to the lower bound. It is more likely that deviations from the inference model assumed by BAYESASS have led to errors in the estimation of the migration rates. The observed bimodality matches the results from Faubet et al. (2007) who noted, based on simulated data, a tendency of the MCMC to get trapped near the bounds of the prior distribution. My literature study shows that these problems are also present when BAYESASS is used to estimate migration rates from empirical data.

It is possible to distil some recommendations from the results presented here. Though these do not guarantee correctness of the migration rates produced by BAYESASS, they should help to make the inferences more reliable. These recommendations partly overlap with those of Faubet et al. (2007), but as those have received surprisingly little follow-up, they are well worth repeating.

Sample few populations, many individuals. Often, researchers are faced with a trade-off to be made between either sampling many populations with a few individuals or a few populations with many individuals. For estimating migration rates using BAYESASS, my literature study makes clear that the best results are obtained with a few populations and many individuals. The number of migration rates to be estimated increases quadratically with the number of populations, which means that sampling many populations gives more room for errors. Furthermore, these results can be understood when considering that BAYESASS works by detecting individuals with recent migrant ancestry, but at the same time also assumes low migration rates; low migration rates simply cannot be estimated using sample sizes of about 20 individuals as there will be no individuals with migrant ancestry in such small samples. Nevertheless, 32% of the population samples were of 20 individuals or less. To make sure that enough individuals with migrant ancestry are included in the sample, sample sizes have to be much larger than that.

Don’t use BAYESASS when population structure is weak. There was a significant relationship between the quality of the analysis and FST. This makes sense in the light of the assignment process underlying the method: when there is little differentiation in allele frequencies among populations, it becomes difficult to assign individuals to populations with any certainty. Note however that there may be many different processes that determine the values of FST, such as migration, mutation (Meirmans & Hedrick 2011), genetic drift and historical processes (Marko & Hart 2011). All these processes may have different effects on the performance of BAYESASS.

One of the best ways to detect convergence problems is to perform multiple repeat runs of the MCMC. The more repeats are run, the more likely it is to find a run that has converged properly. Using modern computers, the calculation time needed for this should not be problematic for most data sets. Surprisingly, the literature study did not reveal any significant effect of the number of repeats. This is probably caused by the fact that the studies that did use multiple runs differed widely in the way that they handled the results from the runs.

When the results of multiple repeat runs are widely different, it is very tempting to NONCONVERGENCE IN MIGRATION ESTIMATION 731 take the average migration rates over repeats and use these values for interpretation. This should never be done. Runs that have not converged properly do not present any useful information and including these results in an average will only introduce error. This is because the frequency with which the MCMC gets trapped near the bounds of the prior distribution is unlikely to be proportional to the actual (correct) migration rate, but rather depends on the shape of the likelihood surface. Therefore, it is better to use an optimality criterion to select the best repeat and use those results for interpretation.

Use the Bayesian deviance. (2007) found that, when calculated for each run, the Bayesian deviance can be used quite effectively as an optimality criterion to find the run that provides the best fit. However, there were only three studies out of the hundred that used the deviance to select the best run. Its low adoption rate is probably due to the fact that BAYESASS does not provide the deviance in its output, and calculating it by hand may be daunting for most users. To promote the use of the deviance, I included an R-script to calculate the deviance from the trace file produced by BAYESASS with the supplementary data of this study (Appendix S1).

Clearly and comprehensively describe the used parameters. Reproducibility is one of the most important aspects of any scientific study. However, many of the included studies were unnecessarily vague in their description of the inference performed using BAYESASS. Many authors simply stated that they performed multiple repeats to ‘look for convergence’ without specifying how the repeats were compared or whether there actually was any consistency among repeats. There were 19 studies that did not mention which version of the software was used, and three studies did not give the number of steps in the MCMC. Similar problems with the reproducibility of the results have been noticed before (Gilbert et al. 2012) for genetic clustering analyses using the program Be realistic about inferences of migration rate. Most importantly, an inference of migration rates –be it with BAYESASS or any other method– should never be done as an afterthought or simply because it is possible. It is nowadays very simple (and I sincerely believe it should be) to input any data at hand into a statistical program and obtain some results. However, every statistical method works best when the experiment has been designed especially around it; conversely, a method cannot be expected to give any valid results when the data is unsuitable – even though this data can be converted into the correct input file format for the method. For one thing, BAYESASS cannot be expected to give any useful insights from a wide-range exploratory analysis of population structure. A typical study of that kind has about 20 populations of 20 individuals sampled from across the whole range of a species. In such a case, it is highly unlikely that any of these samples will contain individuals with migrant ancestry, stemming from exactly the other sampled populations. Therefore, there is no use in trying to estimate migration rates using assignments. For example, it is very unrealistic to assume that a sample of ten rats from Key Largo includes any recent migrants from San Francisco. So, when a migration estimate of 15% is given (Lack et al. 2012), one should seriously question the applicability of the method. It is important to remember that the strength of an analysis depends on its weakest link; in many cases this is the sampling as that is generally the most expensive part of genetic studies. Using many repeat runs in combination with the deviance in a BAYESASS analysis is not going to give any valid results if when the spatial distribution of the samples is unsuitable or when simply insufficient individuals are sampled. In such cases, it may be advisable to forego highly specific analyses such as BAYESASS and use more general –more descriptive– methods of inference.
